name: Spirit's historical progress through nations toward freedom
plain_explanation: Hegel claimed history is not random but shows Spirit gradually coming to know and free itself, moving through three great stages: the East, where only one person (the despot) is free; Greece and Rome, where some people are free; and the German world, where (Hegel claims) all are free -- though his idea of 'freedom' turns out to mean little more than obedience to law.
precise_definition: Hegel's thesis, developed in The Philosophy of History, that history is 'the discipline of the uncontrolled natural will, bringing it into obedience to a universal principle and conferring subjective freedom,' unfolding through three phases (Oriental despotism: one is free; Greco-Roman: some are free; German: all are free), with each historical epoch led by a single 'world-historical' nation carrying the mission of that stage of the dialectic, embodied at times in 'world-historical individuals' (heroes) such as Alexander, Caesar, and Napoleon who may justifiably violate ordinary moral rules.
why_it_mattered: It gives history unity and meaning as a rational, purposive process, and provides the philosophical scaffolding for treating the contemporary Prussian/German State as, in some sense, the near-culmination of world-historical development.
historical_origin: The Philosophy of History (lectures, published posthumously).
examples: Hegel's claim that 'The German spirit is the spirit of the new world'
German history divided into three periods (to Charlemagne; Charlemagne to the Reformation; Reformation onward) styled as the Kingdoms of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
Hegel's naming Alexander, Caesar, and Napoleon as world-historical 'heroes'
objections: Russell: it is 'odd that a process which is represented as cosmic should all have taken place on our planet, and most of it near the Mediterranean.'

Russell: there is no reason, on Hegel's own view that reality is timeless, why later stages of history should embody 'higher' categories than earlier ones -- unless one absurdly supposes the Universe is 'gradually learning Hegel's philosophy.'

Russell notes Hegel's philosophy of history required, like other such theories, 'some distortion of facts and considerable ignorance' -- for instance ignoring the atrocities of the Peasants' War while dating the 'Kingdom of the Holy Ghost' from that period.
competing_positions: Marx's later materialist philosophy of history, which replaces Spirit with economic class conflict but retains the dialectical, nation/class-driven structure
influence_on_later_thinkers: Profoundly shaped later philosophy of history, Marx's historical materialism, and (via Bismarck-era German historians like Mommsen and Treitschke) German nationalist historiography.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: it identifies the German (specifically, implicitly Prussian) State as the nearly-final embodiment of freedom and Spirit, and reinterprets 'freedom' as essentially the right to obey law.
